questions.question: Human African trypanosomiasis is caused by haemoflagellates of which genus?
questions.explanation: Human African trypanosomiasis (HAT) is caused by haemoflagellates of the genus Trypanosoma, specifically T. b. gambiense and T. b. rhodesiense.

questions.question: Human African trypanosomiasis is transmitted by flies of which genus?
questions.explanation: HAT is transmitted by flies of the genus Glossina — the tsetse fly. Both male and female flies can transmit the parasite, unlike mosquitoes.

questions.question: The acute form of HAT is distinguished by fever, adenitis, rash, and what else?
questions.explanation: The acute form of HAT is distinguished by fever, adenitis (swollen lymph nodes), rash, and transitory oedemas — temporary swelling of the face and hands.

questions.question: The chronic form of HAT appears when which system is invaded?
questions.explanation: The chronic form appears when the parasite invades the central nervous system, causing neurological signs including the characteristic sleep disturbances.

questions.question: HAT occurs in some how many sub-Saharan countries?
questions.explanation: HAT occurs in some 36 sub-Saharan countries, across a belt that spans from Senegal in the west to Uganda and Tanzania in the east.

questions.question: HAT is the only vector borne parasitic disease limited to which continent?
questions.explanation: HAT is the only vector-borne parasitic disease limited to the African continent — its distribution is entirely determined by the range of the tsetse fly.

questions.question: Trypanosoma brucei gambiense is distributed in which part of Africa?
questions.explanation: T.b. gambiense is distributed in West and Central Africa, where it causes the chronic form of HAT.

questions.question: Which country has both T.b. gambiense and T.b. rhodesiense?
questions.explanation: Uganda is the only country where both T.b. gambiense and T.b. rhodesiense occur. The two forms are separated geographically by the Victoria Nile.

questions.question: T.b. gambiense is transmitted by which tsetse fly group?
questions.explanation: T.b. gambiense is transmitted by the Palpalis group of tsetse flies, which breed near rivers and lakes and prefer human blood meals.

questions.question: T.b. rhodesiense is transmitted to man by which tsetse fly group?
questions.explanation: T.b. rhodesiense is transmitted to man by the Morsitans group of tsetse flies, which inhabit savannah woodland and feed on wild animals and cattle.

questions.question: T.b. rhodesiense is maintained in wild animals, making it what?
questions.explanation: T.b. rhodesiense is maintained in wild animals, making it a zoonosis — a disease transmitted from animals to humans. Humans are incidental hosts.

questions.question: Which subspecies is more virulent in man?
questions.explanation: T.b. rhodesiense is more virulent in man, causing an acute disease that progresses over weeks or months, whereas T.b. gambiense causes a chronic infection.

questions.question: T.b. brucei is not pathogenic to humans because it is lysed by what?
questions.explanation: T.b. brucei is lysed by a heptoglobin-like molecule in human serum — a trypanosome lytic factor that protects humans from this animal subspecies.

questions.question: The whole life cycle of Trypanosoma brucei lasts about how long?
questions.explanation: The whole life cycle of Trypanosoma brucei lasts about 30 days — from ingestion of bloodstream trypomastigotes by the fly to development of metacyclic forms that can infect a new host.

questions.question: When Glossina takes a blood meal, it ingests which forms?
questions.explanation: When Glossina takes a blood meal from an infected mammal, it ingests bloodstream trypomastigotes — the form circulating in the mammalian host.

questions.question: In the fly midgut, trypanosomes transform into which stage?
questions.explanation: In the fly midgut, trypanosomes transform into the procyclic stage — a replicating form adapted to the insect environment.

questions.question: The only stage infective to vertebrates is what?
questions.explanation: The metacyclic trypomastigote is the only stage infective to vertebrates. It develops in the fly's salivary glands and is injected during a bite.

questions.question: An infected tsetse fly remains infective for how long?
questions.explanation: An infected tsetse fly remains infective for about 3 to 4 months — the remainder of its natural lifespan.

questions.question: The genus Glossina includes about how many known species?
questions.explanation: The genus Glossina includes about 30 known species, divided into three groups based on their habitat and behaviour.

questions.question: Glossina is divided into how many groups?
questions.explanation: Glossina is divided into three groups: Palpalis (riverine), Morsitans (savannah), and Fusca (forest). Only the first two groups include vectors of HAT.

questions.question: Only which groups contain vectors of T.b. gambiense?
questions.explanation: Only the Palpalis and Morsitans groups contain vectors of T.b. gambiense. The Fusca group feeds mainly on forest animals and is not a significant vector.

questions.question: Transmission of trypanosomes depends on Glossina density, longevity, susceptibility, and what else?
questions.explanation: Transmission depends on Glossina density, longevity, susceptibility, and human behaviour — specifically, how often humans enter fly-infested areas and how much skin they expose.

questions.question: Humans are the main reservoir of which subspecies?
questions.explanation: Humans are the main reservoir of T.b. gambiense. The disease is anthroponotic — it maintains itself in the human population without needing an animal reservoir.

questions.question: The key determinant of Gambian HAT epidemic potential is what?
questions.explanation: The key determinant of Gambian HAT epidemic potential is the long duration of infection — years of low-level parasitaemia give many opportunities for tsetse flies to acquire and transmit the parasite.

questions.question: Which human population density is optimal for HAT to prosper?
questions.explanation: Intermediate human population density is optimal for HAT — dense enough to provide blood meals for flies, but not so dense that the disease burns through the population quickly.

questions.question: T.b. rhodesiense is sporadically transmitted to humans who venture into what?
questions.explanation: T.b. rhodesiense is sporadically transmitted to humans who venture into bush infested by tsetse flies — hunters, fishermen, and tourists are at highest risk.

questions.question: Cattle are the major reservoir of which trypanosomiasis?
questions.explanation: Cattle are the major reservoir of rhodesiense trypanosomiasis. Infected cattle serve as a source of parasites for tsetse flies that then bite humans.

questions.question: Rhodesiense trypanosomiasis is mainly an occupational disease of whom?
questions.explanation: Rhodesiense trypanosomiasis is mainly an occupational disease of adult men — hunters, fishermen, and herdsmen whose work brings them into contact with tsetse-infested bush.

questions.question: Rhodesiense trypanosomiasis shows higher incidence during which season?
questions.explanation: Rhodesiense trypanosomiasis shows higher incidence during the warmer season, when tsetse fly activity is greatest and more people venture into bush for farming and fishing.

questions.question: Gambiense HAT is chronic, with signs appearing after how long?
questions.explanation: Gambiense HAT is chronic — signs appear after months or years of silent infection. This long latency is why it spreads readily through communities before being noticed.

questions.question: Rhodesiense HAT progresses over what period?
questions.explanation: Rhodesiense HAT progresses over weeks or months — an acute, rapidly fatal disease if untreated, in contrast to the chronic Gambian form.

questions.question: HAT is classified into how many clinical stages?
questions.explanation: HAT is classified into two clinical stages: stage 1 (haematolymphatic) and stage 2 (meningoencephalitic), depending on whether the CNS is involved.

questions.question: The first stage of HAT is also called what?
questions.explanation: The first stage of HAT is also called the haematolymphatic stage — the parasite is confined to the blood and lymphatic system.

questions.question: The primary lesion at the site of infecting bite is called what?
questions.explanation: The primary lesion at the site of the infecting bite is called a chancre — a painful, indurated, red swelling that appears about a week after infection.

questions.question: Winterbottom's sign refers to enlargement of which lymph nodes?
questions.explanation: Winterbottom's sign refers to enlargement of the posterior cervical lymph nodes — a classic sign of Gambian HAT, first described by Winterbottom in 1803.

questions.question: Fever in Gambian HAT is recurrent and lasts how many days?
questions.explanation: Fever in Gambian HAT is recurrent, with each febrile episode lasting 1 to 3 days, followed by afebrile intervals of days to weeks.

questions.question: In the second stage, what rhythm disappears?
questions.explanation: In the second stage, the circadian sleep rhythm disappears — the hallmark of "sleeping sickness." Patients are drowsy by day and restless at night.

questions.question: Abnormal movements in the second stage include what?
questions.explanation: Abnormal movements in the second stage include tremors of the hands and fingers, choreiform (dance-like) movements, and fasciculations — all signs of CNS involvement.

questions.question: HAT control relies on reducing the parasite reservoir and reducing what?
questions.explanation: HAT control relies on reducing the parasite reservoir (through case detection and treatment) and reducing man-fly contact (through vector control and traps).

questions.question: For T.b. gambiense, reduction of the human reservoir is limited by low sensitivity of what?
questions.explanation: Reduction of the human reservoir is limited by the low sensitivity of standard parasitological techniques — parasitaemia is often too low to detect reliably.

questions.question: Case detection has been the cornerstone of HAT control and relied on what?
questions.explanation: Case detection has relied on examining for swollen cervical lymph nodes (Winterbottom's sign), which can be punctured and examined directly for trypanosomes.

questions.question: Lymph node fluid is examined for evidence of what?
questions.explanation: Lymph node fluid is examined microscopically for trypanosomes — motile, flagellated organisms that confirm the diagnosis.

questions.question: In the 1970s, which test was most reliable for epidemiological surveillance?
questions.explanation: In the 1970s, the Indirect Fluorescent Antibody Test (IFAT) was the most reliable test for epidemiological surveillance of HAT.

questions.question: IFAT was supplanted by which test?
questions.explanation: IFAT was supplanted by CATT (Card Agglutination Test for Trypanosomiasis) — simpler, faster, and not requiring a fluorescence microscope.

questions.question: CATT is which type of test?
questions.explanation: CATT is a latex agglutination test — it uses trypanosome antigens coated on latex particles that agglutinate in the presence of specific antibodies.

questions.question: CATT results are available within how many minutes?
questions.explanation: CATT results are available within 10 minutes — making it suitable for field use and mass screening in endemic areas.

questions.question: Confirmation of diagnosis depends on demonstrating trypanosomes in blood and what?
questions.explanation: Confirmation of diagnosis depends on demonstrating trypanosomes in blood or cerebrospinal fluid. CSF examination is essential to determine the stage of the disease.

questions.question: Which test is most sensitive for detecting blood parasites?
questions.explanation: The mAECT (mini Anion Exchange Centrifugation Technique) is the most sensitive test for detecting blood parasites — it concentrates trypanosomes from large volumes of blood.

questions.question: Before insecticides, vector control depended on eliminating what?
questions.explanation: Before insecticides, vector control depended on eliminating wooded vegetation — clearing bush to destroy tsetse fly resting and breeding sites.

questions.question: Traps should be re-impregnated with insecticide every how long?
questions.explanation: Traps should be re-impregnated with insecticide every 6 months to remain effective. Regular re-treatment is essential for sustained vector control.
